messages.content:
RoadDraft is a headless 2D CAD engine for roadway plans. Model space is US survey feet, and a point is [x, y] = [easting, northing] -- the other way round from how coordinates are usually spoken, so N 7300, E 4100 is [4100, 7300]. Sheets are paper inches seen through viewports at a feet-per-inch scale. Work through the commands: each one validates its params and explains what was wrong, every change is journaled and undoable. Start with get_document_state to see what is in the document, list_commands for the full surface, and render_sheet or render_model to look at your work.

To annotate something, find it before you point at it. In a sheet file the design usually lives in a referenced basefile, so the document owns no geometry of its own; find_entities searches the attachments too. Filter by what a thing IS -- layer, type, or its design anchor -- rather than dumping the document: find_entities {anchor: {kind: 'offset', offset: [-15, 15]}, visible_on: 'P-202'} is the pavement edges that sheet shows. Then pass the id straight to place_callout as target_entity, and the engine puts the leader tip on the geometry. Do not compute the point yourself: the midpoint of a curve's endpoints is not on the curve, and roadway linework runs parallel a few feet apart, so a hand-computed point usually lands on the wrong line rather than on nothing. If you do pass a raw target point, read the warning that comes back -- it names what the tip actually touched.

Some things are not entities at all -- a station, a PC, a point at an offset. Ask the design for those: list_alignments with include_references=true names a referenced alignment 'BASE:RTE-7', and station_to_xy, xy_to_station, resolve_anchor and get_design_data all accept that name and answer in host coordinates. To call one out, give place_callout a target_anchor ('86+50@15R', 'PC-2'; BC-2 and EC-2 name the PC and PT too) and that alignment name. Otherwise commands do not take it: nothing can be drawn, labelled or anchored to an alignment this document does not own.

Plan annotation belongs on the sheet, in paper inches, not in the model. Pass the sheet as place_callout's space and still name a model target -- target_entity or target_anchor: the engine sees it through the sheet's viewport (scale and twist included) and puts the tip where it shows on the paper. 'at' then runs along the part of the entity that sheet shows, since a pavement edge runs the whole project and a sheet shows one stretch. find_entities with visible_on gives each row a sheet_point, which is where that tip will land -- use it to choose a position for the text that is clear of the linework. Never work out a viewport by hand: model_to_sheet and sheet_to_model convert, and station_to_xy and point_on_entity take a sheet and answer in paper inches as well.

Drafting from a description works the same way: give the engine the description, not coordinates you worked out. A bearing and distance goes in as written -- create_alignment takes start + legs (each leg a bearing, azimuth or deflection and the distance to the next PI, with the radius of the curve at the PI it starts from), draw_traverse draws lines and curves course by course, and traverse computes the points without drawing. offset_entity copies linework parallel at a distance (one entity, or a chain offset as one path), fillet rounds the corner between two lines with a curve (a curb return), and measure with along gives distances along a line, chain or alignment and square off it. key_points and snap give the exact endpoints, intersections, centers and alignment design points (PI, BC, EC) to build on. Station-and-offset drafting is draw_station_offset with the stations and offsets given ('82+00@15R'). Linework drawn through something is cut back with trim (a point on the part to cut away) or run on with extend, not redrawn from computed points; break, join, lengthen, chamfer, copy, rotate, mirror, scale and array edit what is there. create_points sets COGO points, label_segments letters bearings and distances or L1/C1 tags with line and curve tables, place_along sets blocks or points at an interval, hatch fills an area (a point inside is enough), and area and get_entity read areas, lengths, bearings and curve data off the drawing.

Do one drafting task in a headless CAD engine called RoadDraft, using the tools you have been given. They are your ENTIRE tool surface.

Rules:
- Every change to the drawing must go through a tool call.
- The document is already open and saves itself after each command. Do not save it under another name.
- Nobody can answer questions. Work until you judge the task done, then stop and give your report.
- You have no calculator and no code execution. Any arithmetic you need, do yourself.

THE TASK:
Create alignment OAK-CT: it begins at N 2000.00, E 3000.00, station 10+00, and runs due north for 400.00 ft. Draw its centerline on layer align_MAIN. It ends in a cul-de-sac: on layer rd_EP draw the bulb, a 45 ft radius circle centered on the end of the alignment, and the edges of pavement 14 ft either side of the centerline, from the beginning to where they meet the bulb -- not through it.

When finished, reply briefly with:
1. What you created and drew (names, layers, key coordinates).
2. The tool calls that mattered, in order (tool name + the key arguments).
3. Anything that failed, confused you, or that you had to work around -- quote error messages. If you had to compute coordinates yourself, show the arithmetic.

messages.reasoning:
Let's analyze this task:

1. Create alignment OAK-CT:
   - Start point: N 2000.00, E 3000.00 → in the format [x, y] = [easting, northing], [3000, 2000]
   - Station 10+00 (start point station)
   - 400.00 feet due north → 400 feet in the +Y direction
   - End point: [3000, 2400]

2. Draw the centerline on layer align_MAIN.

3. The end point becomes a cul-de-sac (loop-the-loop):
   - On layer rd_EP, draw a 45-foot-radius bulb-shaped circle centered on the alignment's end point [3000, 2400]
   - Edges of pavement at 14 feet on each side of the centerline (offsets -14 and +14), from the start point to the location where they meet the bulb (not passing through)

Let's think about the pavement edges. The centerline goes from [3000, 2000] to [3000, 2400], due north. The pavement edges are vertical lines at x = 3000 ± 14, i.e., [2986, 2000] to [2986, ?] and [3014, 2000] to [3014, ?].

Where do they meet the bulb? The bulb is a circle of radius 45 centered on [3000, 2400]. The edge at x = 2986 (14 feet left of the centerline, offset -14) meets the circle when (2986 - 3000)² + (y - 2400)² = 45², i.e., 14² + (y-2400)² = 45². So (y-2400)² = 2025 - 196 = 1829. √1829 ≈ ?

√1829: 42² = 1764, 43² = 1849. So between 42 and 43. 42.7² = 1823.29. 42.8² = 1831.84. 42.76² = 1828.42. 42.77² = 1829.27. So √1829 ≈ 42.7668...

Let me compute more precisely: 42.76² = 1828.4176. 1829 - 1828.4176 = 0.5824. Derivative 2×42.76 = 85.52. 0.5824/85.52 ≈ 0.00681. So √1829 ≈ 42.7668.

The edges meet the circle on the lower side of the circle (before passing through it). The pavement edges run north from station 10+00 (y=2000) and meet the circle at y = 2400 - 42.7668 ≈ 2357.2332.

Hmm, but wait — the typical cul-de-sac: the pavement edges taper into the bulb. But the task says "edges of pavement at 14 feet on each side of the centerline, from the start point to where they meet the bulb — do not pass through." So the edges are straight lines at 14 feet on each side, cut off at the location where they touch the bulb circle. That is, each edge goes from y=2000 to y ≈ 2357.23.

Options:
1. Use draw_offset with alignment OAK-CT, offsets [-14, 14], station_range [10+00, station where it meets the bulb]. The station where it meets: the offset lines meet the circle at y = 2357.2332, so the station is 10+00 + (2357.2332 - 2000) = 10+00 + 357.2332 = 13+57.23.

Hmm, but draw_offset draws the offsets between stations — on a straight line the offset is just a parallel line, ending exactly at the stations. With station_range [0, 357.23], the offset lines go from y=2000 to y=2357.23. That works!

But wait — there's a subtle point: is the "meeting point" exactly on the circle? Yes: the offset line at x=2986 intersects the circle of radius 45 centered at (3000, 2400) at y = 2400 ± √(45²-14²) = 2400 ± 42.7668. The edge stops at the lower intersection point y = 2357.2332 (station 13+57.2332).

2. Or, draw the full-length offset lines and trim them with the circle. That's the "draftsman" approach: draw offsets for the full length, then trim with the circle as the boundary. Actually, trim cuts at the location where the target crosses the boundary — the offset lines cross the circle at two points (lower at y=2357.23, upper at y=2442.77). With trim, if I specify "the portion to be removed" as a point on the part to be cut, I can leave the portion from the start point up to the first intersection. This is a clean approach: offset the full length, then trim each edge at a point on the far side of the circle.

Actually, let me think about which is more robust. draw_offset with station_range requires computing the exact station 13+57.2332, which I can compute. But then the offset line's end is exactly on the circle. With trim, the engine computes the intersection exactly — no manual computation needed. The guidance says "don't compute coordinates by hand," and I should let the engine compute intersections. Let's do this:

1. create_alignment OAK-CT, pis [[3000, 2000], [3000, 2400]], start point station "10+00". Wait — start and end points: pis requires at least 2 points. [3000, 2000] is the start, [3000, 2400] is the end. A straight line, no curve. Start point station 10+00.

Actually, I can also use legs: start [3000, 2000], legs [{bearing: "N 0°00'00\" E", distance: 400}]. Either works. Let's use pis — it's simpler. Due north = +Y. End point [3000, 2400].

2. draw_alignment OAK-CT, layer align_MAIN. Need to first create the layer align_MAIN (create_layer) — or it might be auto-created. Let me check the document state first. For safety, I'll create the layer explicitly.

3. Create layer rd_EP.

4. Draw bulb: draw_circle, center [3000, 2400], radius 45, layer rd_EP. The center is the alignment's end point. I can also confirm with get_design_data or key_points alignment=OAK-CT that END is [3000, 2400].

5. Draw pavement edges: draw_offset, alignment OAK-CT, offsets [-14, 14], layer rd_EP. This draws the full-length edges (10+00 to 14+00, i.e., y=2000 to y=2400).

6. Trim the edges at the circle: find the edge entity ids (returned by draw_offset), then trim targets [{id: edgeL, at: [2986, 2420]}] — a point on the portion past the circle to be removed. The circle is the boundary (the default is all linework in space). The edge line crosses the circle at y=2357.23 (entry) and y=2442.77 (exit). The portion to remove is from y=2357.23... no wait, the offset line goes from y=2000 to y=2400 (the full length of the alignment). It only crosses the circle once in that range: at y=2357.23 (entry point). Because the line ends at y=2400 which is inside the circle (distance from center 0 < 45). So trim with at at [2986, 2380] (a point on the part past the intersection, to be removed) leaves the portion from y=2000 to y=2357.23.

Wait, but the edge lines end at y=2400 (station 14+00). The intersection with the circle at y=2357.23 is inside the line. Trim cuts at the intersection and removes the portion containing at=[2986, 2380], i.e., from y=2357.23 to y=2400. The remaining part: y=2000 to y=2357.23.

This is exactly "from the start point to where they meet the bulb — do not pass through."

But wait — should I draw the edges as full length and then trim, or is there a subtle issue: the offset chain — draw_offset draws lines/arcs as anchored entities. On a straight alignment, each offset is one line. No problem.

As an alternative, use station_range with the computed station. I'd need to do the √1829 computation. Trim is cleaner and exact — the engine computes the intersection. Let's go with trim.

Hmm, one consideration: after trimming, the edge lines are anchored (drawn from the alignment) — "design linework retains anchors and is re-stationed" (from the trim description). Good.

Also to consider: should the edges meet the circle exactly? After trim, the line ends exactly at the intersection with the circle. Yes.

Now, let me also consider whether to first confirm the END point. I can verify that the end point is [3000, 2400] with key_points alignment=OAK-CT. But since I defined the pis, it's exactly [3000, 2400]. Still, for safety (and to show diligence), I can query it. The circle is drawn at the computed point, so I need to be confident. Let's verify with key_points or get_design_data kind=anchors.

Plan of tool calls:

1. get_document_state (summary) — see what's there.
2. create_layer align_MAIN (color black or something), create_layer rd_EP.
3. create_alignment name OAK-CT, pis [[3000, 2000], [3000, 2400]], start point station "10+00".
4. Verify the end point: key_points alignment OAK-CT (or get_design_data kind anchors).
5. draw_alignment alignment OAK-CT, layer align_MAIN.
6. draw_circle center [3000, 2400], radius 45, layer rd_EP.
7. draw_offset alignment OAK-CT, offsets [-14, 14], layer rd_EP.
8. Find the edge entity ids (returned in draw_offset's response).
9. Trim each edge with at a point on the part inside/past the circle.
10. Verify: render_model, or check the entities. Render the model at the bounds around the drawing and look at it.

Let me think about the trim at points:
- Left edge (x=2986, i.e., 14 feet left of northbound centerline... wait: the direction is north (+Y). Left of north is west (-X). So offset -14 → x=2986 (west side). Offset +14 → x=3014 (east side).
- Left edge line: from [2986, 2000] to [2986, 2400]. Circle intersection: y = 2400 - √(45²-14²) ≈ 2357.233 (lower) and 2442.77 (upper, beyond the line's end). Trim: remove the portion from y≈2357.233 to 2400. A point on that portion: [2986, 2380].
- Right edge: [3014, 2000] to [3014, 2400]. Same. at [3014, 2380].

But I need the actual entity ids from draw_offset's response. They should be listed. Let's do that.

Actually, wait. A subtle point: trim uses "all lines, polylines, arcs, and circles in the space" as boundaries. The centerline and offset lines are all there. The offset line crosses the centerline? No — the offset lines are parallel to the centerline, they don't cross. They cross the circle at y=2357.233. Good, a single intersection within the line's range. Trim with at=[2986, 2380] removes everything from that intersection to the end.

One more consideration: should I also close the bulb — that is, draw a circle (the whole bulb) — yes, the task says to draw a 45-foot-radius bulb circle. So the entire circle.

Does "meet the bulb" mean tangent to the circle's edge — yes, the endpoints of the offset lines lie exactly on the circle after trim.

Also to consider: does the task want the pavement edges to start from station 10+00 (start point) — yes, "from the start point."

Now, let me double-check draw_offset's behavior with station_range: not needed, I'll trim.

Let me also consider whether draw_offset draws two separate line entities or one polyline with two sub-paths. It probably returns two entity ids (one per offset). If it's one polyline containing both... unlikely — offsets are separate chains. Let's see the response.

Text/labels: not requested. No stationing labels are needed. Keep it minimal.

Let me also double-check the alignment: "400.00 feet due north" — from [3000, 2000] to [3000, 2400]. Bearing N 0° E. End point station = 10+00 + 400 = 14+00.

Potential pitfall: create_alignment's pis — "([x, y] at start/end, [x, y, R] for interior)." Two points, both without radius → straight line. Good.

Order of operations — independent calls in parallel where possible:
- First, get_document_state (alone).
- Then, create_layer ×2, create_alignment — these are independent of each other. But does create_alignment require the layer? No, the layer is only needed for drawing. Can I run create_alignment and create_layer in the same block? They're independent. Yes.
- Then, key_points/verify the end point + draw_alignment + draw_circle — draw_alignment requires the alignment to exist; draw_circle requires knowing the center (I have it). key_points is read-only. Can be batched: draw_alignment, draw_circle, key_points.
- Then, draw_offset (requires the alignment).
- Then, trim (requires the offset entity ids from the previous response).
- Finally, verify: render_model at the bounds, and get_document_state summary if needed.

Let me write out the arithmetic for the report:
- √(45² − 14²) = √(2025 − 196) = √1829 ≈ 42.7668
- Intersection y = 2400 − 42.7668 = 2357.2332 → station 13+57.23 (display station = 10+00 + 357.2332 = 13+57.2332)

Let me compute √1829 more carefully:
42.7² = 1823.29
42.8² = 1831.84
Interpolate: need 1829. 1829 - 1823.29 = 5.71; 1831.84 - 1823.29 = 8.55. 5.71/8.55 = 0.6678. So ≈ 42.7668.
Check 42.7668²: 42.7668² = (42.7668)². 42.7668 × 42.7668: 42.7668 × 42 = 1796.2056; 42.7668 × 0.7668 = 32.7938... let me do it properly: 42.7668² = (42.77 - 0.0032)² = 42.77² - 2×42.77×0.0032 + tiny = 1829.2729 - 0.273728 + 0.0000102 = 1829.00018. Excellent, so √1829 ≈ 42.76678. Good.

So the edges stop at y ≈ 2357.2332, i.e., station 13+57.23.

Now, do I even need to state this? Trim computes it for me, but I'll mention it in the report as a check.

messages.reasoning:
Empty document. The layers align_MAIN and rd_EP already exist. What I need to do:

1. Create an alignment OAK-CT: starting from N 2000.00, E 3000.00 = [3000, 2000], station 10+00, running due north (azimuth 0) for 400.00 ft. So the endpoint is [3000, 2400].

For create_alignment I can use start + legs: start [3000, 2000], legs: [{bearing: "N 0°00'00\" E", distance: 400}]. Hmm, or azimuth 0. A due-north bearing: "N 0° E" or azimuth 0. Let me use azimuth: 0, distance: 400. Actually a due-north bearing is "N 0°00'00\" E". Let's use azimuth 0.

2. Draw the centerline with draw_alignment on layer align_MAIN.

3. Draw the bulb: on rd_EP, a 45-ft-radius circle centered at the end of the alignment [3000, 2400].

Wait — a 45-ft-radius circle centered on the endpoint? If the endpoint is at the center of the circle, the circle extends 45 ft past the endpoint (to y=2445). Normally a bulb is tangent to the pavement edges. But the task says "45-ft-radius bulb circle centered on the end of the alignment." So center = endpoint = [3000, 2400], radius 45. I'll follow the instructions literally.

4. Pavement edges 14 ft to the left and right of the centerline, from the start point to where they meet the bulb — not passing through it.

The centerline runs from [3000, 2000] to [3000, 2400] (north). 14 ft to each side: x = 3014 (right/east side) and x = 2986 (left/west side).

Where do the pavement edges meet the bulb? The bulb is a circle of radius 45 centered at [3000, 2400]. A vertical line x = 3014 meets the circle where (3014-3000)² + (y-2400)² = 45² → 196 + (y-2400)² = 2025 → (y-2400)² = 1829 → y - 2400 = ±√1829.

The circle is centered at 2400 with radius 45, so the south end of the circle is at y = 2355. The line x=3014 intersects the circle at y = 2400 ± 42.767 → y = 2357.23 (south side, closer to the start point) or y = 2442.77 (north side). The south-side intersection y = 2357.23 is on the near side of the bulb. So the edges should end there.

Now, how to draw the edges "to where they meet the bulb" with a tool? Options:

Option A: Use draw_offset with station_range. The alignment runs 10+00 to 10+400. Distance along from the start where x=3014 meets the circle: station = 2000 + (y - 2000) → y = 2357.233 → station 10+357.23. So draw_offset offsets [-14, 14], station_range [1000, 10357.23]. Hmm, station_range draws only between the display stations. This gives edges from the start point to station 10+357.23, i.e., y = 2357.23. This is exactly the intersection point. So √1829 is between 42.76 and 42.77. 1829 - 1828.4176 = 0.5824; gap per 0.01 is 1829.2729-1828.4176 = 0.8553. 0.5824/0.8553 ≈ 0.681. So √1829 ≈ 42.7668. Let me check 42.767² = (42.77 - 0.003)² = 1829.2729 - 2*42.77*0.003 + 0.000009 = 1829.2729 - 0.25662 + 0.000009 ≈ 1829.0163. Slightly over 1829. So √1829 ≈ 42.7666. Check 42.7666²: 42.7666² = (42.76 + 0.0066)² = 1828.4176 + 2*42.76*0.0066 + 0.0000436 = 1828.4176 + 0.564432 + 0.0000436 ≈ 1828.98208. Hmm, that's less than 1829. Difference: 1829 - 1828.98208 = 0.01792. Derivative 2*42.7666 ≈ 85.53 per unit, so add 0.01792/85.53 ≈ 0.000209. So √1829 ≈ 42.76681.

So y = 2400 - 42.76681 = 2357.23319. Station = 1000 + (2357.23319 - 2000) = 10357.23319 → "10+357.23".
